# Characters

Notion-style cartoon people: thick black-and-white ink lines, at most one accent color, bust (head + shoulders).
**All characters are generated by the same code; they differ only in their "spec" parameters.** Never write separate drawing code for one particular character.

## 1. When to use characters

- When talking about **specific people** (scientists, historical figures, inventors), use a character instead of a name sticky note.
- When you need a **questioner** to voice the audience's doubts ("But why...?").
- When a problem walkthrough needs a **teacher**.
- Videos that purely explain a phenomenon or concept with no people in them **can skip** characters. Don't use them just for the sake of it.

## 2. From any person to a spec: feature extraction

Viewers recognize a cartoon person by the **silhouette** and one or two **signature features**, not by facial details.
Extract in the order below, **taking only the single most recognizable point for each item**; leave items with nothing distinctive at their defaults:

1. **Age group**: kid / adult / elder. Affects face proportions, wrinkles and eye size.
2. **Silhouette** (most important): hairstyle outline, length, texture, or a hat. Ignore facial features; ask only whether the outline alone is recognizable.
3. **Facial markers**: beard / mustache, glasses. Use them if the person has them; otherwise don't add any.
4. **Clothing**: shows the era or profession, e.g. a cravat for an early-modern European scholar, a lab coat for a scientist, a hoodie for a student.
5. **One accent color**: on the clothes, tie, hair ornament or hat. One accent color per character.
6. **Signature prop** (optional): something not in the parts library but essential to this person; draw it with a custom part.

After extracting, ask yourself first: **from the black-and-white silhouette alone, can viewers tell who this is / what role this is?** If not, strengthen items 2 and 3 rather than adding more detail.

## 3. Spec reference

```js
// characters.js
window.CAST = {
  Name: {
    age: 'adult',            // kid | adult | elder
    face: 'oval',            // oval | round | long | square | heart
    nose: 'hook',            // hook | small | round | long | button
    hair: {
      style: 'side-part',    // side-part | middle-part | bangs | slick | spiky | afro | bun | ponytail | buzz | receding | bald
      length: 'short',       // none | short | medium | shoulder | long (hair hanging down at the back)
      texture: 'straight',   // straight | wavy | curly | coily | messy
      color: 'black',        // black | brown | gray | white | blonde | red | any color value
    },
    facialHair: [],          // combinable: mustache | walrus (big mustache) | beard | goatee | stubble | wisp (three-strand long beard: thin mustache + a tuft on the chin; ancient scholars, elders)
    facialHairColor: 'gray', // defaults to the hair color if omitted
    glasses: 'none',         // none | round | square | sunglasses
    hat: 'none',             // none | top-hat | cap | beret | bow | headband | guan (small crown on the topknot; ancient officials, literati) | mian (mian crown with bead tassels; emperors)
    earrings: false,
    outfit: { style: 'tshirt', color: 'white' },
      // style: tshirt | vneck | scoop | collar | suit | cravat | turtleneck | hoodie | labcoat | robe (cross-collar robe, right lapel over left)
      // color: white | black | accent | any color value; suit can add tie, labcoat can add shirt, robe can add trim (collar edging color, defaults to the accent color)
    accent: '#D6342C',       // accent color
    parts: [],               // custom parts, see section 4
  },
};
```

**Style constraints**: hair is mostly solid black fill; light hair (white, gray, blonde) automatically gets hair-strand lines; clothes use at most one color; no realistic skin tones — keep faces white.

## 4. Custom parts

Things missing from the parts library (headscarf, crown, a pencil behind the ear, a special hairstyle...) are drawn as SVG paths in the character's **local coordinate system**:

- Face center is (0, 0); face width is about 140 (x from -70 to 70)
- Top of head y ≈ -100, chin y ≈ 95, eyes (±26, -2), mouth (0, 56)
- Base of neck y ≈ 128, bottom edge of the bust y = 230, outer edge of shoulders x = ±150

```js
parts: [
  { layer: 'top', d: 'M-60,-110 L-40,-150 L0,-120 L40,-150 L60,-110 Z', fill: '#E0B000' },  // e.g. a crown
]
```
`layer` values: `hairBack` (behind the head), `body` (on the clothes), `hairFront` (in front of the hair), `top` (topmost layer).
Stroke width defaults to 5 and color to black; change them with `stroke` and `width`. Writing `'accent'` for `fill` / `stroke` uses this character's own accent color,
so the same prop (e.g. a sword) can be reused as-is by different characters.
Parts on the `hairBack` layer are hidden behind the body and head, which suits things that "peek out from behind the shoulders" (a sword on the back, a quiver, a scroll).
Always check the position on the model sheet afterwards.

## 5. Putting it in the video

```js
const c = b.character(CAST.Name, { x: 1650, y: 1080, size: 380, at: T.start('intro'), flip: false });
```
- `x, y`: position of the **bottom-center** of the bust. y is usually the bottom edge of the frame or region, so the character "stands" on the edge.
- `size`: height in pixels, usually 300–420.
- `flip: true`: mirror horizontally so the character faces the content.
- The entrance works like any other whiteboard element: it is drawn stroke by stroke (1.8 seconds by default).

### Actions
| Call | Effect |
|---|---|
| `c.expr(at, 'think')` | Switch expression, 0.3 s smooth transition |
| `c.expr(at, { lookX: 1 })` | Change only some parameters (partial override) |
| `c.look(at, x, y)` | Eyes look in a direction (-1 to 1) |
| `c.say('id')` / `c.say(['id1','id2'])` | These narration lines are "spoken" by this character: the mouth opens and closes to the per-word timing |
| `c.say('id', { from: 'any', to: 'attract' })` | Speak only a span of this line (when the narration goes "he said: ...", only the quoted part is spoken by the character) |
| `c.nod(at)` | Nod |
| `c.point(at, x, y, { hold: 1.5 })` | Raise the arm (shoulder → elbow → hand) and point at world coordinates (x, y) on the board; when the target is below, point horizontally instead. If the previous point hasn't been lowered yet, the new point turns directly from the current pose (waving, switching direction) instead of lowering and raising again |
| `c.hold(at, x, y, prop, { hold })` | Point at (x, y) holding a prop (sword, pointer, torch, magnifying glass...). Equivalent to `point(at, x, y, { prop })`; subsequent `point` calls keep holding it as long as the hand hasn't been lowered |
| `c.handAt(t)` | The hand's position and orientation on the board at time t, `{ x, y, angle }` (null when the hand is not raised). Use it when another element should start from the hand (something handed over, a line shot out); **don't replicate the arm math yourself** |
| `c.move(...)` `c.erase(...)` `c.pulse(...)` | Same as for other elements |

Blinking, breathing and slight swaying while speaking are automatic.

**Props** (`prop`) are part lists just like `b.sketch` (strings, or `{ d, fill, stroke, width }`), drawn at world size (pixels):
**origin = where the hand grips, +x direction = the direction toward the target**. The prop is drawn under the hand, which "grips" on top of it; it fades in when the arm rises and fades out when the arm lowers.
```js
// Sword: hilt behind the grip point, crossguard slightly in front of it, blade along +x
const SWORD = [
  { d: 'M-40,-6 L0,-6 L0,6 L-40,6 Z', fill: 'ink' },            // hilt
  { d: 'M0,-22 L12,-22 L12,22 L0,22 Z', fill: 'accent' },        // crossguard
  { d: 'M12,-9 L200,-9 L226,0 L200,9 L12,9 Z', fill: '#EEF2F7' }, // blade
];
c.hold(T.word('dance', 'sword') - 0.1, 900, 300, SWORD, { hold: 1 })  // raise the sword
 .point(T.word('dance', 'Liu Bang'), 1000, 700, { hold: 1.2 });       // swing toward the other side, sword still in hand
```

**Expressions**: `neutral` `smile` `happy` `explain` `think` `surprised` `confused` `sad` `serious` `proud` `excited`
Expression parameters (for partial overrides): `eyeOpen` `eyeSize` `lookX` `lookY` `happyEyes` `browL` `browR` `browTilt` `mouthCurve` `mouthOpen` `mouthWidth` `mouthShift` `tilt`

## 6. Acting principles

- **Characters are supporting cast**: place them at the edge or corner of the frame, never covering the content being explained; usually only one character per frame.
- **Expressions follow the story beats**: `think` or `confused` when posing a question, `surprised` then `happy` at the reveal, `explain` while explaining.
- **Gaze guides the audience**: when new content appears, have the character `look` or `point` at it. Viewers follow the character's gaze.
- **Only `say` on the character's own lines**: open the mouth only when the narration is relaying this character's words ("his answer was..."); when the narration is describing him, he should keep his mouth shut and act with expressions.
- **When two or more characters share a frame** (dialogue, standoff), use `flip` to make them face each other; for each line only the speaker `say`s, the other reacts with an expression.
- **Don't move constantly**: at most one obvious action per line (pick one of expression change, point, nod); let the automatic blinking and breathing "carry" the rest.

## 7. Process

1. Write the specs in the project's `characters.js`.
2. Render model sheets: `node scripts/cast.mjs <project>` shows all characters; `node scripts/cast.mjs <project> <name>` shows one character's full set of expressions, speaking, and pointing in four directions (upper right, left, lower right, straight up).
3. **Show new characters' model sheets to the user for confirmation first**, then put them in the video.

## 8. Spec examples (examples only; design each video's own characters with the method in section 2)

```js
{ age: 'kid', face: 'round', nose: 'button', hair: { style: 'ponytail', color: 'black' }, hat: 'bow', outfit: { style: 'tshirt', color: 'accent' }, accent: '#E07B00' }   // kid asking questions
{ face: 'oval', nose: 'small', hair: { style: 'bangs', length: 'medium' }, glasses: 'round', outfit: { style: 'collar' } }                                              // teacher
{ age: 'elder', hair: { style: 'spiky', length: 'medium', texture: 'messy', color: 'white' }, facialHair: ['walrus'], outfit: { style: 'collar', color: '#9A9A9A' } } // white-haired old professor
{ face: 'long', nose: 'long', hair: { style: 'middle-part', length: 'shoulder', texture: 'curly' }, outfit: { style: 'cravat', color: '#8B5A3C' } }                   // 17th-century European scholar
{ age: 'elder', hair: { style: 'bun', length: 'none' }, facialHair: ['wisp'], hat: 'guan', outfit: { style: 'robe' }, accent: '#1E8A4C' }                          // ancient Chinese civil official / strategist
{ face: 'square', hair: { style: 'bun', length: 'none' }, facialHair: ['beard'], hat: 'mian', outfit: { style: 'robe' }, accent: '#D6342C' }                         // ancient Chinese emperor
```
**Several characters from the same era** (all wearing the same clothes): differentiate them through item 2, the silhouette (guan / mian / topknot only), and item 3 (beard or not, which kind of beard),
then give each one an accent color; if they still can't be told apart, add a signature prop.
